claude.sample_unit: medical reports (100 reports rated by 9 experts)

links.outcome: Ability of clinician experts to identify AI-generated versus human-written reports as a proxy for review
links.effect: Experts identified report origin with 0.60 accuracy (near chance), while an automated classifier reached 0.98; human verification called an increasingly unreliable safety control.
links.quote: Overall accuracy ranged from 58% to 61% (0.60 per average) across document types and languages.

links.outcome: Report accuracy, fluency, completeness against source EHR using automatic metrics and expert Likert ratings
links.effect: Phi-4 ROUGE-1 0.70, BERTScore 0.83; expert ratings overall 4.6/5 (accuracy 4.4-4.9, completeness 4.6-4.8).
links.quote: Quality evaluation by 9 medical experts in 100 medical reports resulted in most scores exceeding 4.0/5.0 in the 5-point Likert scale, with accuracy ranging from 4.4 to 4.9, fluency from 4.0 to 4.5, and completeness from 4.6 to 4.8.

links.outcome: Detection of AI-generated reports by automated classifier versus human experts
links.effect: EuroBERT classifier achieved overall accuracy 0.98 versus experts 0.60, supporting automated detection tools for provenance.
links.quote: As shown in Table 3 , in contrast to human experts, the machine learning-based classifier leveraging EuroBERT 18 achieved a robust detection performance with an overall accuracy of 0.98 ( P < 0.001).

links.outcome: Generated report quality in English versus French
links.effect: Comparable ROUGE/BERTScore across languages; natively authored French reports accuracy 4.9/5, but machine-translated French transcripts fluency 4.0 versus 4.5 English.
links.quote: In contrast, machine-translated French transcripts scored significantly lower in fluency (4.0/5.0) compared to their English counterparts (4.5/5.0).

unlisted_practices: Automated detection classifiers for AI-generated text to audit provenance of clinical documentation
